A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same 105-task benchmark, renamed from SecureAgentBench to SecureVibeBench. All 27 pages of v1 and 19 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable, and retained methods, examples, tables, and results can be matched.

before.justification: Section 3 reports original agent evaluations, cost and vulnerability analyses, and an experiment with explicit security reminders.

after.justification: Sections 4–5 report agent evaluations, additional CLI-agent results, a manual SAST audit, and comparisons of alternative security-risk reference settings.

M1.justification: The benchmark retains B-SZZ candidate selection, three-commit dynamic validation, GPT-4.1 requirement generation, Dockerized patch-generation tasks, and functional and security oracles. Describing the existing construction as cascading analysis and renaming PoC to PoV do not establish an algorithm change.

E1.justification: The 105 C/C++ tasks, 41 projects, and historical vulnerability coverage remain. However, v2 removes the explicit-security-reminder input scenario evaluated in v1 Section 3/Figure 7 and documented in Appendix G, retaining the default security-neutral coding prompt.

E2.justification: v2 retains the three original agent frameworks and three backbones, adds Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5 for each framework, and evaluates Claude Code with Sonnet 4.5 and Codex with GPT-5 in Section 5/Table 4. This substantially expands the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: The stated Semgrep scope changes from over 26,000 rules to over 2,400 community and Pro rules, despite retaining version 1.137.0; this establishes revised protocol documentation, not that experiments were rerun. v2 also regroups six outcome categories into four, changes per-CWE percentages from a correct-output denominator to all samples in that CWE, and adds manual-audit and gold-patch-reference evaluation protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds a manual SAST false-alarm audit, an absolute-versus-gold-patch-relative security analysis, runtime analysis, and a concrete context-window failure case for harfbuzz task 58663. It removes the security-reminder experiment. The rawspeed example and its contrasting agent patches are retained through relocation.

E5.justification: v2 Section 5 introduces sampling-based estimation of SAST false alarms using 40 randomly selected flagged snippets per agent, reported as 120 programs overall. Single-run agent evaluation remains unchanged: neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests for its own agent results.

E6.justification: The nine original secure-solution scores are retained, while newly evaluated configurations introduce substantial additional results. The best reported score becomes 23.8% for SWE-agent with Sonnet 4.5, versus v1's 15.2% for SWE-agent with DeepSeek-V3.1. v2 Table 4 lists Codex at 19.0% and Claude Code at 17.1%, although the prose orders these scores inconsistently. Additional findings include 16 suspicious CWE categories versus 14 previously, audit outcomes, and 4.9% versus 2.6% suspicious rates under different reference settings.

T1.justification: Neither version develops a formal theoretical model, theorem, proof, or mathematical derivation. The revised empirical outcome categories and new discussion of test adequacy do not introduce formal theory.

C1.justification: The central benchmark contribution and conclusion that agents struggle with secure coding remain. v2 makes fair human–agent comparison more explicit, changes the novelty claim from the first combination of three benchmark features to the first repository-level multi-file-editing secure-coding benchmark, and drops the headline conclusion about ineffective security reminders.

C2.justification: v2 gives scaffold design greater importance in cost-effectiveness and explains Aider failures through context-window overload. It adds substantive interpretations of SAST false alarms and human-reference comparisons, arguments about functional-test adequacy and contamination, and an explicit benchmark-size limitation. The earlier security-reminder mechanism explanation and associated training recommendations disappear.

D1.justification: v2 Appendix B adds community/Pro rule access instructions, rule-set details, and an example rule; Appendix C.2 adds DeepSeek's parameter count and an expected $5,000 computational budget. Existing hardware, agent versions, and per-task limits remain. v1's benchmark repository link and code/data release commitment disappear without replacement access information.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantial comparison with concurrent SusVibes, positioning vulnerability-introduction reconstruction and new-risk detection as distinguishing features. Table 1 adds SusVibes and A.S.E., while Appendix A adds discussion of Agentless, PatchPilot, and Refact.ai. New software-practice citations support the test-oracle rationale; these are positioning additions, not evaluated baselines.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and substantial portions of the benchmark and results narratives are rewritten. Related work moves before the benchmark description, results gain separate functionality and security subsections, and discussion, limitations, ethics, and appendices are reorganized. Terminology changes include the benchmark name and PoC/PoV.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout and substantially redesigns the displays. It removes the task illustration, construction diagram, security-reminder chart, and dataset histograms; adds runtime and failure plots plus a CLI-results table; and redraws the overall-results and CWE charts. Retained code examples and prompts are reflowed, with the requirement-generation prompt split across pages.

improvement.justification: Broader agent comparisons, the concrete failure case, and direct examination of SAST validity improve empirical support and interpretation beyond v1's largely aggregate analysis and generic SAST caveat. The gains are limited by removal of the security-reminder study and benchmark access information, inconsistent CLI-score attribution relative to Table 4, and audit percentages that do not reconcile with the stated 120-program sample.
